content: An online Delphi consultation was conducted with a group of experts specializing in transgender health and HIV to identify and reach a consensus on the most critical topics to include in in-depth interviews. The Delphi method is a structured process that gathers and refines expert knowledge through a series of questionnaires, with responses summarized and shared for controlled feedback. This consultation was carried out in two rounds using an electronic survey platform, SurveyMonkey. In the first round, summarized responses were shared with participants, and a second questionnaire was distributed, excluding questions where consensus had already been achieved. The World Health Organization (WHO) regional offices were informed about the Delphi consultation and asked to provide contacts for key regional experts in transgender health and HIV. Using these contacts, along with prominent experts from academia and international organizations, 44 individuals were invited via email to participate in the Delphi exercise. A week after the initial invitation, a 27-item survey questionnaire was sent out, remaining open for one week, with a reminder email sent a day before closure. Respondents were anonymous to one another, and only the research team had access to participant details. Responses were analyzed using descriptive statistics. Based on the analysis of Round 1, a second survey was developed, summarizing items where consensus (defined as 51% agreement) had been reached. The second survey was sent to the 24 experts who participated in Round 1, along with a summary of the results. The survey remained open for one week, with a reminder email sent before closure. Eighteen experts participated in Round 2, representing a 75% response rate among Round 1 participants. After analysis, participants were informed of the Round 2 results. For the in-depth interviews, transgender participants were recruited using a convenience and snowball sampling method. Experts contacted through the Delphi process were asked to provide contact details of transgender individuals from their networks or regions to participate in the interviews. Based on these contacts, 72 transgender individuals were identified and personally invited via email. Additional recruitment was conducted through advertisements on social media, organizational networks, and mailing lists. Thirty-five transgender networks and organizations, representing major regional and local transgender networks and NGOs, were contacted and asked to forward the invitation to their members. The recruitment letter included a link to a short online survey where transgender individuals could register their interest in participating by providing basic sociodemographic information. Thirty-four individuals completed the survey. To ensure equal regional representation and capture diverse perspectives regarding age, gender, transition stage, and HIV status, 19 transgender individuals were invited to participate in interviews. Fourteen agreed, and interviews were arranged individually. These interviews were conducted in December 2013 and January 2014 by an independent consultant via telephone or Skype. A semi-structured interview guide, developed based on the Delphi consultation and scoping review results, was used to guide the discussions. Topics included HIV knowledge, prevention, testing, counseling, treatment, care, antiretrovirals as prevention, and other health concerns. Open-ended questions encouraged participants to share personal experiences, opinions, and perspectives in depth. At the start of each interview, the interviewer verbally reviewed the participant information sheet, which had been sent to participants beforehand, and obtained verbal consent. Interviews lasted between 50 and 90 minutes and were conducted in English, except for one conducted in Spanish with the assistance of a translator. All interviews were recorded and transcribed verbatim by the consultant. Information from the interviews and the short online survey was anonymized, with only the consultant having access to personal details of participants. The transcribed interviews were entered into the qualitative analysis software QDA Miner Lite. Each interview was re-read and thematically coded using the software. Coding was organized based on the topics covered in the interview guide, with additional themes and topics emerging from the data also included. Content for each code or theme was retrieved separately, and all quotations related to a specific theme or code were re-read and analyzed for content. A narrative section for each theme was then written. The demographic and psychosocial profiles of the 14 transgender individuals interviewed are summarized in tables. Eleven were transgender women, and three were transgender men. Participants came from Brazil, El Salvador, Fiji, France, India, Indonesia, the Philippines, the Russian Federation, Singapore, South Africa, Thailand, and the United States, representing five WHO regions. No participants from the Eastern Mediterranean region could be identified for the interviews. Ages ranged from 22 to 60 years. All but one participant worked with transgender or health-related organizations. Three participants were living with HIV and receiving antiretroviral therapy (ART), eight reported being HIV-negative, and three did not know their HIV status. Of these three, two had never been tested for HIV. Key findings from the interviews highlighted that friends and the transgender community were the primary sources of HIV and health-related information, providing peer support and fostering a strong sense of community. Information was exchanged both face-to-face and virtually. The Internet and social media were also significant sources of information, with many participants actively seeking information on hormone use, gender-affirming surgery, healthcare services, and providers. However, information specific to HIV was less frequently sought online. Participants emphasized the importance of validated information from government, UN agencies, and academic research, which could be adapted to local contexts. Challenges included a lack of transgender-specific information and research, particularly on hormone use and its interactions with HIV prevention, risks, and treatment. Many participants felt marginalized within the broader LGBT community and expressed frustration with the conflation of transgender issues with those of men who have sex with men (MSM). Some also noted that HIV discourse in their contexts was predominantly targeted at heterosexuals, neglecting transgender-specific issues. Participants called for more research on transgender-specific health issues and the development of targeted, accessible information that does not exclude non-English speakers, illiterate individuals, or those without Internet access.
